verdict: OK to lend selectively to Kandla-Gandhidham port-linked operators with clean receivables and contracted cargo; avoid commodity-price-exposed, single-client stevedoring and CFS units until receivables and cost pass-through are verified.
title: Kandla-Gandhidham Ports & Port Services: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A port-services borrower in Kandla-Gandhidham earns by moving cargo, not by owning the sea.** Stevedoring, CFS/warehouse handling, barge and tug operations, and logistics yards convert labour, equipment and berth time into per-tonne or per-TEU fees. Cash arrives after the cargo owner or trader settles, so the working-capital cycle is the business. **The value sits in berth access, handling contracts and receivable quality, not in the fixed assets.**

## What has changed now
**Peer results are strong: APSEZ Q2 FY27 revenue rose 23.7% to ₹11,340 crore and net profit 16.5% to ₹3,622 crore, with EBITDA margin at 60% [2][3].** But a separate Emkay note says persistent cost inflation is partly offsetting volume growth across logistics and ports in Q2 FY27 [4]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's per-tonne realisation has kept pace with its cost inflation; if margins are flat while volumes rise, ask for the cost pass-through clause in the handling contract.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue operators tied to contracted, diversified cargo and to the larger port ecosystem that is visibly expanding [1][2].** Target CFS and yard operators with multi-client books, barge/tug owners with fixed-hire contracts, and logistics providers serving the port's hinterland. **Avoid single-client stevedores and traders' captive CFS units where one commodity price swing moves the whole receivable book.** Rating reports show receivable periods of 57-60 days at healthy port operators [5][8]; **if a proposal shows receivables materially above that, ask for the ageing and the top-five debtor list before sanction.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the cycle, not the peak.** Keep tenors short, match limits to the working-capital cycle, and take monthly stock-and-receivable statements plus bank statements. **Take a charge on receivables and a promoter guarantee; if the borrower's operating cycle exceeds the peer range of 51-60 days [5][6][8], ask for a monthly receivables ageing covenant.** Note that the data pack gives no city-level score, so this call rests on first principles and peers, not local statistics [D].

## Early-warning signs
**Watch debtor days, cargo concentration and cost pass-through.** If debtor days stretch beyond the peer range [5][8], ask for the top-five debtor ageing and hold fresh limits. If one client crosses a third of billings, ask for the contract tenure. If fuel or handling cost rises without a matching tariff revision [4], ask for the revised rate card. **Rating reports flag tax claims and regulatory capex as real risks in this sector [6][8]; if a tax demand or regulatory notice appears, ask for the provision and the cash impact.**
watch: Monthly bank statements and receivable ageing (monthly)
Debtor days above 60 [5][8] -> hold fresh limits and ask for top-five debtor ageing
Volumes up but margin flat [4] -> ask for cost pass-through clause and revised rate card
Single client above one-third of billings -> ask for contract tenure and diversify condition
Any demand or notice [6][8] -> ask for provision and cash impact before renewal
